title: The Supreme Court is about to take a closer look at Trump’s immigration agenda | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’simmigration agendawhen they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.

The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president’sasylum ban, his vast expansion ofmandatory detentionof migrants and his push to send certain people in the US illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some withdubious human rights records.

Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.

Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer’s blockbuster decisionupholding birthright citizenship, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are “indispensable” to its overall immigration crackdown.

“In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law,” said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. “These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.”

Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the1798 Alien Enemies Actto quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

On the other hand, six-justice majorities in Juneallowed Trump to enda form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.

“If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name,” she said.

Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration’s immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-electPeggy Flanaganvowed to “rip ICE apart.” New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker,told CBSthat Democrats would “put an end to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine.”

But Republicans havealready frontloaded fundingfor ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White Housechief of staff— a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.

“It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. “Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court.”

Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president’s program.

“Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned,” Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.

Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.

“Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term,” he predicted, “I think it’s doing the same kind of cleanup.”

The showdown will begin on December 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump’s push to remove certainmigrants to countriesother than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

Federal law allows such “third country” removals in cases when a migrant’s home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants’ rights groups.

In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the “third country,” even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.

Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won’t be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.

The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket,three times allowedthe administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.

Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration’s decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.

That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration’s ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.

Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump’s first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.

And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump’s asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.

US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, warned the court of a “vicious cycle” that encouraged “illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would ‘be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.’”

But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.

In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the “most important and effective” policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, “threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half.”

The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.

Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm’s way.

“These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate US immigration law as it has been understood for decades,” said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.

“If the court validates the policies,” he said, “it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the US asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation’s commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms.”

The story headline has been updated.
